query:
What exists today (weight post-2025 sources heavily) across these five areas, and does any of it publish per-entry tested verdicts with honest failures?

1. Prompt or technique libraries that publish evaluation results per individual entry
2. Versioned prompt registries with test suites attached
3. 'Prompt pack' marketplaces — and the documented reasons buyers do or do not trust them
4. Public benchmarks for creative, divergent, or open-ended LLM output quality
5. Retraction and changelog practices in prompt-engineering communities

Deliver two things: (a) a landscape matrix covering who each player is, what they publish per entry, what evidence standard they hold themselves to, and where the gaps are; (b) a directly cited answer to the question 'does any existing library publish per-entry tested verdicts that include honest failures and public retractions?'

Map the research lineage behind LLM divergence mechanisms, weighting papers and credible documented practice from 2024-2026. Cover three areas:

1. LLM output homogenization and mode collapse in creative and open-ended tasks — including studies measuring whether brainstorming with LLMs reduces idea diversity across individuals and groups.

2. Techniques shown to increase output diversity or novelty: structured prompting protocols, persona and frame forcing, adversarial or critic/multi-agent setups, temperature and sampling interventions versus prompt-level interventions, and corpus or context injection.

3. Ported human creativity techniques — structured brainstorming methods (e.g. SCAMPER, Six Thinking Hats, morphological analysis, analogical/design-by-analogy transfer) applied through LLMs — and any measured results.

Deliverable: a cited map of which divergence-mechanism families have real EVIDENCE behind them versus which are folklore or untested practitioner lore. For each family state what was measured, on what task, with what diversity metric, effect size or direction if reported, and the strength of the evidence. Be explicit about which claims rest on a single small study, which replicate, and where measurement itself is contested (i.e. how 'diversity' and 'novelty' are operationalized and whether those metrics are trusted).

What do the academic literature and authoritative practitioner sources from 2024-2026 identify as the core competencies, frameworks, and recurring failure modes of systems thinking as applied to AI product management? Cover four areas with citations: (1) Which classical systems-thinking frameworks (Meadows' leverage points, Senge's system archetypes, causal loop diagramming, stock-and-flow modeling, the iceberg model) have documented, non-trivial applications to AI/ML product development — who applied them and what happened. (2) Which AI-specific system dynamics are documented and measured: data flywheels, model/data drift, degenerate feedback loops in recommender systems, eval and retraining loops, human-AI preference feedback loops (e.g. RLHF-driven distribution shift), and agentic/multi-agent system dynamics. (3) What competencies and practices do credible sources recommend for product managers to develop systems-thinking judgment for AI products, and which pedagogical approaches (exercises, simulations, case teardowns, spaced practice) have evidence behind them. (4) Which documented AI product failures (named incidents, post-mortems) are attributed by credible analysis to systems-level causes rather than component failures. Deliverable: (a) a competency map an AI PM curriculum could be built from, distinguishing evidence-backed items from practitioner folklore; (b) a list of load-bearing topics that standard treatments of 'systems thinking for PMs' tend to omit, each with why it matters and a source.

What do peer-reviewed research and authoritative primary engineering sources from 2024-2026 establish about structured methods for reasoning about the architecture, failure modes, and design trade-offs of AI/LLM-based software systems, and about how such reasoning is taught and assessed? Cover four areas with citations.

(1) FAILURE-ANALYSIS METHODS: Named, documented analytical frameworks for decomposing a system and systematically anticipating how it fails - FMEA, STPA/STAMP, fault-tree analysis, HAZOP, chaos engineering, pre-mortem/prospective hindsight, threat modeling (STRIDE). For each: its actual procedure, its evidence base, and any documented adaptation to machine-learning or LLM-based systems specifically. Which of these have been genuinely adapted to AI systems by credible parties, and what did the adaptation change?

(2) FAILURE TAXONOMIES FOR AI SYSTEMS: Documented, empirically-grounded taxonomies of how retrieval-augmented generation, tool-calling/function-calling, and agentic systems fail in production. Prefer measured studies and incident analyses over vendor blog posts. Include retrieval failure modes, context/grounding failures, orchestration and multi-agent failure modes, evaluation failures (including LLM-as-judge bias and reward hacking), and drift.

(3) TACIT-TO-EXPLICIT EXPERTISE: What does expertise and learning-science research establish about how practitioners who already possess substantial hands-on tacit skill convert it into explicit, articulable, transferable expert reasoning? Cover cognitive task analysis, think-aloud/verbal protocol analysis, case-based reasoning, deliberate practice, worked-example and faded-scaffolding effects, self-explanation, and the documented expertise-reversal effect. What specifically is known about training fluent verbal articulation of technical reasoning under time pressure, as distinct from training the underlying competence?

(4) ASSESSMENT: What is documented about what technical and AI product-management interviews actually assess in system-design and architecture rounds - the evaluation rubrics, the observable signals interviewers report using, and any published research on the validity of these assessments.

Deliverable: (a) a synthesis of which structured method or combination is best supported for a practitioner reasoning about AI system architecture and failure; (b) an explicit separation of evidence-backed claims from practitioner folklore; (c) what standard treatments of this material typically omit.

What do the peer-reviewed software engineering, requirements engineering, and human-computer interaction literatures (2015-2026) establish about the design and decision responsibilities in machine-learning and LLM-based product development, and what would a defensible, ordered decision procedure for a non-engineer product owner of such a system contain? Prioritize peer-reviewed venues (ICSE, FSE, CHI, CSCW, NeurIPS, TSE, RE, EMSE) and authoritative primary sources over practitioner blogs. Cover five areas with citations.

(1) VALIDATED PROCESS AND LIFECYCLE MODELS. Empirically-derived process models for ML/AI system development: Amershi et al.'s nine-stage workflow (ICSE 2019), CRISP-DM and its ML/AI successors, MLOps maturity models, and LLM-application-specific lifecycle models published 2023-2026. For each: how it was derived, what evidence supports it, which design and requirements activities it specifies BEFORE implementation, and where empirical studies show teams actually deviate, skip steps, or fail.

(2) REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING FOR ML (RE4AI). What this literature establishes about specifying requirements, acceptance criteria, and non-functional requirements for probabilistic systems: how performance targets and error budgets get negotiated; how false-positive versus false-negative cost asymmetry is elicited and specified; how data requirements are captured; and the documented consequences when these are left implicit. Include systematic reviews and any validated artifacts, templates, or checklists.

(3) HUMAN-AI INTERACTION DESIGN CANON. Amershi et al.'s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019): how it was derived, its validation methodology, and subsequent replication or critique. Google's People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft's HAX toolkit: provenance and evidence status. Research on communicating uncertainty and confidence to users, designing for AI error and recovery, explanation and trust calibration including documented over-trust and under-trust effects, and Wizard-of-Oz and prototyping methods for probabilistic systems. Separate what is empirically validated from what is asserted.

(4) SYSTEMIC RISK AND TECHNICAL DEBT. Sculley et al.'s Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (NeurIPS 2015) and its successors: the documented structural anti-patterns (entanglement/CACE, hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependency debt, glue code, pipeline jungles, configuration debt), which have been empirically confirmed or challenged since, and what detection or audit methods exist. Include any adaptation to LLM and agentic architectures.

(5) DIVISION OF LABOR. What research documents about which decisions in AI system development are actually owned by product and other non-engineering roles versus engineering, where the handoffs empirically fail, and what competencies studies identify as necessary for the product-side role.

DELIVERABLES: (a) an ordered decision procedure - the sequence of questions a product owner should work through when designing or evaluating an AI system - with each step justified by cited evidence, and explicit notes wherever the literature disagrees or is silent; (b) a competency map separating what is empirically validated from what is practitioner assertion; (c) the most commonly documented omissions and failure points in how product people reason about AI systems.

What do first-person practitioner accounts, team postmortems, industry surveys, conference talks, and academic or industry literature from 2024-2026 document about how AI/LLM product teams govern OFFLINE evaluation while iterating on prompts, models, and configurations? Exclude vendor product-feature marketing; prioritize accounts of what teams actually do and what goes wrong. Cover four areas with citations: (1) HOLDOUT DISCIPLINE: documented practices and incidents around held-out or sealed evaluation sets for LLM features — do teams maintain a split their iteration loop cannot see, and what documented cases exist of teams overfitting to their own eval set (offline scores rising while production quality did not)? (2) CHANGE ISOLATION: is one-change-at-a-time iteration practiced when tuning prompts/models, what do practitioners report happens when multiple changes are bundled, and what vocabulary do teams use for this discipline (champion/challenger, A/B of versions, ablation)? (3) SHIP/NO-SHIP DOCUMENTATION: how do real teams document and review decisions to promote an AI quality change — decision records, approval workflows, audit trails, rationale requirements — and what do practitioners and governance/compliance sources say about gaps when no such record exists? (4) ROLE DIVISION: what do practitioner accounts and surveys document about the split between product managers and engineers in operating eval workflows — which parts PMs own, where PMs report being blocked by tooling or by engineering dependency, and any accounts of PMs wanting but lacking direct control of eval iteration. Deliverable: (a) a cited synthesis distinguishing documented team practice from aspirational best-practice advice; (b) named incidents or first-person accounts for each area where they exist; (c) an explicit note on which of the four areas has the thinnest real-world evidence.
